title: Iran War Updates: Tehran proposes 7-day plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz as it seeks deal before U.S. midterms
text:
Stated Claim / Post Context:
Iran War Updates: Tehran proposes 7-day plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz as it seeks deal before U.S. midterms

Iran's president says Tehran wants a deal with the U.S. before November's midterm elections, as the regime puts an offer on the table.

Actual Article Body:
Watch CBS News

Updated on:  September 25, 2026 / 1:11 PM EDT
            / CBS News

Oil prices retreated slightly Friday on reports of potential overtures toward ending the U.S.-Iran war, which helped support stock prices after a volatile week.

Wall Street indices opened higher following slight gains in Europe and a mixed performance in Asia, against a backdrop of rising government bond yields and persistent inflation fears.

After falling sharply on hopes of a breakthrough to end the Middle East war during the U.N. General Assembly in New York this week, oil prices jumped when there were no initial signs of progress.

But they fell back modestly Friday, with international benchmark Brent crude trading at about $103 per barrel at midday, down about 2.5% from Thursday, after Iran's foreign minister said the country had submitted an offer to Washington that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz to tanker traffic within seven days if an agreement is reached.

"If certain conditions are met, the strait will be open within seven days and talks will start," Abbas Araghchi told reporters on the sidelines of the U.N. gathering.

"It is a dubious offer considering Iran hasn't changed its conditions from before," said Patrick O'Hare, an analyst at Briefing.com. "We'll see how long the glow of Iran's offer lasts."

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told journalists Thursday that Tehran wanted a peace deal before November's U.S. midterm elections, contradicting claims by President Trump that Iran would only do a deal after the voting.

CBS/AFP

President Trump made it clear to China that any help for Iran, direct or indirect, is "totally unacceptable," according to U.S. Ambassador to China David Perdue.

"We made it very clear to them weeks ago that any help that they would give Iran, whether it be direct or indirect, whether it be intelligence or parts or military equipment, was totally unacceptable," Perdue told CNBC on Friday. "President Trump made that very clear again yesterday."

The U.S. has warned China about helping Iran, and even said they were expected to assist the U.S. in enforcing sanctions on Iran — a request that was immediately rejected by China, Iran's largest trade partner.

Perdue did say the U.S. believes China has provided some support, while indirect, in keeping the Strait of Hormuz closed.

"There's been indirect support, we think, but there's no direct evidence," he told CNBC. "We're very concerned about this indirect work, and we've made that very clear."

President Trump said Friday he had discussed the Iran war with visiting Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping, following allegations Beijing has been supporting Tehran.

"We did, we did," Trump said when asked if they had talked about Iran, as he showed Xi around the National Archives in Washington on the last day of the Chinese leader's state visit.

Asked if he thought there would be progress on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, Trump replied, "I think we're going to do great."

Mr. Trump was asked by the television pool reporter if he had asked Xi to stop sharing intelligence with Iran, but the president ignored the question.

CBS/AFP

Iran-U.S. negotiations in New York have moved beyond initial diplomatic contacts into a more detailed technical phase, with sources in Tehran describing the atmosphere as increasingly positive, Al Jazeera's bureau chief in Tehran, Nourddine Dgheir, reported Friday.

The Qatari-government owned network said technical experts had joined the discussions in New York after a first meeting involving U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. While visas were not initially approved by the U.S. government for the Iranian delegation, they were secured quickly, allowing the team to join the talks, Dgheir said.

There was no immediate confirmation by U.S. officials that the talks had progressed to the technical level, or that additional Iranian officials had been cleared to enter the country.
